summary: Defines fifteen metadata elements for describing resources across fields, known as the Dublin Core Metadata Element Set. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Dublin Core is a shared checklist of fifteen things worth writing down about any resource, from a book to a web page. It gives every one of them a name that people can read and a name that software can use, so that catalogues in different fields can describe things in the same way.

what are the dublin core elements
what is dublin core metadata used for
subtitle: Fifteen simple labels, such as title, creator and date, for describing almost any kind of resource.

tldr.problem: Electronic resources are hard to find unless they carry descriptions in a common vocabulary that works across fields such as libraries, research and publishing.
tldr.mechanism: The Dublin Core Metadata Element Set defines fifteen broad, generic elements (title, creator, subject, date and so on), each with a human label, a machine name, a definition and sometimes a usage comment.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Version 1.1 of the element set. It obsoletes RFC 2413, the first published version, and mainly rewords some definitions.

today: RFC 5013 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2413. No later RFC is listed as replacing or updating it, so the Version 1.1 element set it carries remains the text to consult.

sections.title: Introduction: Where the Element Set Came From
sections.content:
The Dublin Core Metadata Workshop Series began in 1995 with an invitational workshop that brought together librarians, digital library researchers, content experts and text-markup experts to promote better discovery standards for electronic resources. The resulting metadata element set defines fifteen metadata elements for resource description in a cross-disciplinary information environment.

The document carries the current text of Dublin Core Version 1.1. Version 1.1 is the basis of ANSI/NISO Z39.85-2001, and the text of the RFC closely follows the text in the 2007 revision of ANSI/NISO Z39.85, especially sections 2 to 6 and 10 to 12. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2413, which was the first published version of the Dublin Core, Version 1.0.

The main differences between this RFC and RFC 2413 are in the wording of definitions: for Contributor and Date the meaning was broadened, for Relation it was clarified, and redundant references to the content of a resource were removed in general. The RFC also recommends lowercase element names, consistent with RDF property types, stays silent about the unrestrictedness of element ordering and repeatability, on the grounds that application profiles are the proper place to discuss such topics, and refers to the current abstract model, vocabularies and namespace policies in which the Dublin Core is embedded.
sections.plainLanguage: The set was written by librarians and researchers who wanted catalogues in different fields to describe a resource in the same way. This version mainly tidies up the wording of the first one and standardises the spelling of the element names.

sections.title: Scope, Definitions and How Elements Are Named
sections.content:
The element set is a standard for cross-domain resource description. As in RFC 3986, this specification does not limit the scope of what might be a resource. The elements are typically used in the context of an application profile, which constrains or specifies their use in line with local or community-based requirements and policies, and the specification of such implementation detail is outside the scope of the document.

Three definitions matter. DCMI is the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative, the maintenance agency for the element set. A resource is anything that might be identified, the same definition as in RFC 3986 and in the DCMI Abstract Model. The lifecycle of a resource is a sequence of events that mark the development and use of a resource, with the examples given being the conception of an invention, the creation of a draft, the revision of an article, the publication of a book, acquisition by a library, transcription to magnetic disk, migration to optical storage, translation into English and the derivation of a new work such as a movie.

Each element has a descriptive label for human consumption and a unique token for use in machine processing. In accordance with the DCMI Namespace Policy, the name of an element is appended to a DCMI namespace URI to construct a Uniform Resource Identifier that is globally unique for that element, and the use of element names and URIs in different implementation technologies is explained in the DCMI Encoding Guidelines. All changes made to the terms of the element set since 2001 have been reviewed by a DCMI Usage Board in the context of a namespace policy that describes how DCMI terms are assigned URIs and sets limits on the editorial changes that may be made to the labels, definitions and usage comments of existing terms.
sections.plainLanguage: Each element has two names: one people read and one machines use. The machine name is turned into a web address by joining it to a fixed namespace, so that every element has an identifier that is unique everywhere.

sections.title: The Fifteen Elements
sections.content:
The element set is a vocabulary of fifteen properties for use in resource description. The name Dublin comes from its origin at a 1995 invitational workshop in Dublin, Ohio, and core because its elements are broad and generic, usable for describing a wide range of resources.

Eight of the elements describe who made something and what it is about. Title is a name given to the resource. Creator is an entity primarily responsible for making the resource, and the examples given are a person, an organization or a service, with the name of the creator used to identify the entity. Subject is the topic of the resource, typically represented using keywords, key phrases or classification codes, and the recommended best practice is to use a controlled vocabulary. Description is an account of the resource, and may include an abstract, a table of contents, a graphical representation or a free-text account. Publisher is an entity responsible for making the resource available. Contributor is an entity responsible for making contributions to the resource. Date is a point or period of time associated with an event in the lifecycle of the resource, and may be used to express temporal information at any level of granularity, with the recommended best practice being an encoding scheme such as the W3CDTF profile of ISO 8601.

The other seven describe what kind of thing it is and how it relates to other things. Type is the nature or genre of the resource, with the DCMI Type Vocabulary offered as a controlled vocabulary, and the Format element used instead to describe the file format, physical medium or dimensions. Format is the file format, physical medium or dimensions of the resource, where examples of dimensions include size and duration, and the list of Internet Media Types is offered as a controlled vocabulary. Identifier is an unambiguous reference to the resource within a given context. Source is a related resource from which the described resource is derived, in whole or in part. Language is a language of the resource, with RFC 4646 offered as a controlled vocabulary. Relation is a related resource. Coverage is the spatial or temporal topic of the resource, its spatial applicability, or the jurisdiction under which it is relevant, where named places or time periods can be used in preference to numeric identifiers. Rights is information about rights held in and over the resource, typically a statement about the various property rights associated with it, including intellectual property rights.
sections.plainLanguage: The fifteen elements fall into two groups. Eight say who made the resource and what it is about; seven say what kind of thing it is, how to find it and how it relates to other resources.

sections.title: How the Set Fits With the Rest of DCMI
sections.content:
The fifteen elements described in this document are part of a larger set of metadata vocabularies and technical specifications maintained by the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative. The full set of vocabularies, DCMI Metadata Terms, also includes a set of resource classes, the DCMI Type Vocabulary. The terms in DCMI vocabularies are intended to be used in combination with terms from other compatible vocabularies in the context of application profiles, and on the basis of the DCMI Abstract Model.

The memo points readers to the informative references that describe this wider setting: the DCMI Abstract Model, the DCMI Encoding Guidelines, the DCMI Namespace Policy, DCMI Metadata Terms, the DCMI Type Vocabulary, the Internet Media Types list, Resource Description Framework, the Getty Thesaurus of Geographic Names, the W3C date and time formats note, and the ANSI/NISO standards Z39.85-2001 and Z39.85-2007. An appendix adds that the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative is responsible for the development, standardization and promotion of the element set, and points to the organization's web site for information about workshops, reports, working group papers, projects and new developments.
sections.plainLanguage: The fifteen elements are the most used part of a wider set of vocabularies, which also cover types of resource and the rules for giving terms unique names. The RFC lists where to read more about each of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Dublin Core element set poses no risk to computers and networks. It poses minimal risk to searchers who obtain incorrect or private information due to careless mapping from rich data descriptions to the Dublin Core elements, and the memo says no other security concerns are likely.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing metadata does not endanger a computer. The one risk is that a careless mapping puts private or wrong information in a description that people then find.

viz.caption: THE FIFTEEN ELEMENTS AND THEIR DEFINITIONS

cells: A name given to the resource.
An entity primarily responsible for making the resource.
An entity responsible for making the resource available.
An entity responsible for making contributions to the resource.
A point or period of time associated with an event in the lifecycle of the resource.
The nature or genre of the resource.
The file format, physical medium, or dimensions of the resource.
An unambiguous reference to the resource within a given context.
A related resource from which the described resource is derived.
The spatial or temporal topic of the resource, the spatial applicability of the resource, or the jurisdiction under which the resource is relevant.
Information about rights held in and over the resource.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARTS OF AN ELEMENT

items.title: Label
items.text: A descriptive label for human consumption, such as Title or Creator.

items.title: Name
items.text: A unique token for machine processing, such as title or creator.

items.title: Definition
items.text: What the element means, given in one sentence.

items.title: Comment
items.text: Guidance on use, such as which controlled vocabulary to choose.
